transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The Trump administration has announced it is rolling back fuel economy standards for
new vehicles.
It says less efficient vehicles make cars more affordable for Americans.
As NPR's Willett Rubin reports, this is a step that weakens Biden-era climate policies.
The corporate average fuel economy, CAFE standards, have been around since the '70s.
Companies require American carmakers to make each year's new vehicles more fuel-efficient
on average across their entire fleets.
But how much more efficient?
Under the Biden administration, fleets needed to get 2% more efficient every year.
That meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles balance out their gas guzzlers, otherwise
they were subject to a fine.
That fine went away last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Now a much smaller increase in fuel efficiency will be required every year.
Willett Rubin, NPR News.
Voters may soon feel more economic pain.
There are upcoming cuts to safety net programs, such as SNAP.
Along with that, President Trump is going to cut hundreds of millions of dollars from
programs he opposes, even though Congress has approved funding for them.
And bears more Eliasian reports, this is called a pocket veto or pocket rescission.
According to the White House, the canceled funds include over $550 million from programs
that provided services to refugees and other non-citizens.
Later this week, the cuts to Medicaid and food stamp SNAP benefits that were in Trump's
One Big Beautiful Bill are going to kick in.
And this pocket rescission has been called illegal by the General Accounting Office.
So together, all of these cuts add up to more economic pressure on voters.
NPR's Mara Eliasian reporting.
Iran's embassy in London is denying any involvement in a suspected plot that was foiled near an
air base in western England.
It's one of the bases where U.S. military bombers take off for attacks on Iran.
And bears Lauren Freer reports from London.
The Iranian embassy in London says it categorically rejects what it calls malicious speculations
that it was involved in a suspected terror plot near Royal Air Force Base, Fairford.
In the middle of the night, early Sunday, a farmer alerted police to three suspicious
vehicles near that British air base.
Police intercepted them and arrested five men, whom they say are British nationals all in
their mid-20s living in London.
They've been detained on suspicion of both explosives and terrorism offenses.
British counter-terrorism officials say they're aware that "geopolitical questions are being
raised," but that the idea that the base may have been targeted because of its role
in U.S. attacks on Iran is just one of many threads they are investigating.
Lauren Freer, NPR News, London.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The White House has started airing a new ad featuring President Trump.
In it, he asks people to join him in his fight to expel warmongers from government.
The ad says it was paid for by the U.S. government.
This is the second such ad released by the White House in recent days.
Critics say these appear to violate federal law.
Weather forecasters say that the nor'easter that pounded the east coast over the weekend
is now weakening.
One person was killed in New York State by a falling tree this weekend.
The powerful storm brought winds that were near hurricane strength.
It is still pouring rain from New York to New England.
The smoke billowing off a wildfire can travel hundreds or thousands of miles.
A new field of study is trying to understand how that smoke may be disturbing wild places
and creatures, such as birds.
Here's NPR's Ari Daniel.
Having repeatedly experienced wildfire smoke herself, Olivia Sanderfoot, who's based at
Cornell University, has long wanted to know how birds handle it.
It's not just about what they're inhaling, which is inevitably bad for them.
It's also about how the cues that they use to navigate their world are upended when it
gets smoky outside.
Sanderfoot's teamed up with researchers in other disciplines to create a new field called
smoke ecology.
It relies in part on birders already on the ground collecting bird activity data when
smoke happens to blow in.
A top priority is to determine where birds go when it's smoky and what can be done to
help them.
Ari Daniel, NPR News.
listening to NPR
